blocks.title: Goryeong as a growing political centre
paragraphs: Daegaya's later prominence is associated with the Goryeong region and the concentration of imposing elite tombs at Jisan-dong. The development followed changes in the lower Nakdong power balance, but the precise timing and reasons for its rise require more than a claim that one federation simply moved its capital. Local production, alliances and the ability to mobilize communities in adjacent valleys all contributed to potential authority.

The Academy of Korean Studies notes that the same terms Gaya, Gara and Daegaya could refer to different centres in different texts. This creates historical confusion when a chronicle records a Gaya king without specifying which polity. Geographical inference must be tied to dates and source context, while an attractive territorial map should not resolve every ambiguity by assertion. The centre's political strength is visible in both text and archaeology, but the two registers remain distinct.

blocks.title: Jisan-dong and the politics of burial
paragraphs: The Jisan-dong tumuli include exceptionally large burial mounds and rich offerings, which demonstrate the concentration of resources among prominent groups. Their scale implies labour coordination, specialist craft and arrangements for collecting and redistributing goods. Human sacrifice or attendant burial has been discussed for some Gaya elite tombs, raising difficult questions about coercion, rank and ritual obligation.

Burial evidence is not a census of the living. Tombs may represent a narrow elite, and mortuary practices can exaggerate hierarchy or change independently of political institutions. The interpretation of particular skeletons and placements demands archaeological documentation, not a generic statement that every large tomb contained the same ceremony. The cemetery is especially useful when compared with ordinary settlements, agricultural production and regional workshops whose labour supported elite display.

blocks.title: Rulers, titles and symbols of supra-local power
paragraphs: Inscriptions on Gaya-period objects, including terminology rendered as great king, indicate the ambitions of some rulers and their use of prestige language. Such terms tell us how elites wished to be recognized, but do not specify the precise territory or enforceable powers of the person who bore the title. The court could be influential beyond Goryeong without governing every Gaya polity as a province.

A network of subordinate chiefs might supply tribute or troops in exchange for alliance and security. Alternatively, some communities may have balanced Daegaya against Silla, Baekje or another Gaya centre. The historian should distinguish influence from direct administration and acknowledge the possibility of several competing alliances in the same region. The absence of a surviving Daegaya administrative archive sharply limits reconstruction of its court procedures.

blocks.title: Diplomacy across an unstable political landscape
paragraphs: Daegaya operated between larger neighbours whose power was changing in the fifth and sixth centuries. Relations with Baekje could offer routes and military partnerships; relations with Silla might provide security but risk dependence. Sources refer to negotiations and shifting alliances, though chronology and attribution can be problematic.

The court's strategic problem was not solved by one permanent friend or enemy. A community that exported iron or maintained river passages could be economically valuable and militarily exposed at once. Alliances could turn costly if allies pursued territorial expansion of their own. The political trajectory of Daegaya is therefore best understood through a sequence of specific diplomatic choices and changing material capabilities, not a timeless claim that its leaders were predestined to be absorbed by Silla.

blocks.title: A diverse kingdom beneath a royal name
paragraphs: Goryeong's elite centre depended on farming households, craft workers, transporters and people in smaller settlements. The funerary wealth of its rulers should not obscure these populations or imply that all residents identified themselves as members of a single ethnic nation. Regional pottery and burial forms show both shared patterns and significant variation.

A state can integrate a region politically while local customs remain distinct. Craft circulation may reflect exchange rather than permanent migration, and administrative influence may extend only along secure routes. Maps often combine evidence from different decades into a single outline. A more historically honest approach illustrates an expanding sphere of power with uncertain margins and records the evidence behind each proposed identification.

blocks.title: Power in 562 and the problem of sudden endings
paragraphs: The Silla court's conquest of Daegaya in 562 is recorded in the Samguk Sagi, which associates the expedition with Isabu and Sadaham. By then Geumgwan Gaya had already submitted in 532. Confusion between the two events occurs in later transmitted traditions and must be resolved through source comparison rather than by simply choosing the most memorable date.

The loss of independent kingship did not erase the people, crafts and networks of Goryeong. Elites might enter Silla service, communities might retain local practices and material production could continue under new obligations. The dramatic event is the end of one royal authority. The larger history includes the changing conditions that made it possible and the uneven social transformations afterward.
